title: Surface-Code Quantum Error Correction for Molecular Tweezer Arrays: Encoding, Layout, and Correlated Noise
abstract: Polar molecules trapped in optical tweezer arrays offer a promising platform for quantum information processing, providing precise control and long-range interactions that enable high-fidelity gate operations. We investigate quantum error correction in this system and show the influence of underlying physical noise. A mapping is constructed from a molecular tweezer array onto a rotated surface code in which a single specification of the array, namely, which code qubits share a molecule and where those molecules are located, determines both the correlated erasure structure and the dipolar exchange graph. We compare molecular encodings with rotational qudit dimensions (D), two and four under heralded molecular loss, coherent dipolar exchange, and imperfect heralding. It is found that a D= 4 encoding with spatially dispersed pairing exhibits a finite distance crossing at approximately the same per molecule loss rate as D= 2, while using 48-49 % fewer molecules, at the cost of a 6-10 % increase in sub-threshold logical error. Fixing the encoding and varying only the spatial embedding produces substantially larger effects: pairing the two co-located qubits along a lattice direction yields a logical-sector asymmetry of approximately fifty times. Over the simulated distances (d = 5, 7, 9), the disfavoured sector shows little or no suppression of logical error with increasing code distance, whereas the favoured sector improves by a factor of 1.5-2.3. We also find that Pauli twirl of the exchange interaction overestimates the logical error rate, which we attribute to the excitation-conserving structure of the interaction. These results reveal that the spatial embedding of correlated loss units is an important design parameter for molecular architectures and that single-sector benchmarks may be insufficient when correlated loss has directional structure.
summary: This research analyzes quantum error correction on molecular tweezer arrays, demonstrating that the physical layout of the qubits is as critical as the encoding scheme itself. The authors show that spatial arrangement can induce significant directional biases in logical errors, necessitating the use of worst-case sector metrics for robust hardware design. The findings provide actionable design rules for building scalable, fault-tolerant quantum memories.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the physical structure of molecular tweezer arrays influences the performance of surface-code quantum error correction (QEC). It specifically compares different encoding strategies and the impact of spatial arrangement on error suppression.
main_result: Spatially dispersed $D=4$ encodings can achieve comparable error thresholds to $D=2$ encodings while using significantly fewer molecules. Crucially, the spatial embedding structure, rather than just the encoding dimension, dictates whether logical errors exhibit directional asymmetry.
method: The authors constructed a mapping from the molecular array to a rotated surface code, simulating error rates under various noise models, including correlated molecular loss and coherent dipolar exchange.
model_or_system: The platform is polar molecules trapped in optical tweezer arrays, used to implement qubits for a surface code. The system is modeled by considering correlated erasures based on qubit sharing and dipolar exchange interactions ($w_{ij} \propto r^{-3}$).
key_observables: Logical error rate ($P_L$), worst-case logical error ($P_{	ext{worst } L}$), and the degree of logical-sector asymmetry ($P_Z^L$ vs. $P_X^L$).
important_parameters: Code distance ($d=5, 7, 9$), molecular loss rate ($p_{mol}$), and the encoding dimension ($D=2$ vs. $D=4$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to finite code distances, and the comparison of error rates is based on relative trends rather than asymptotic threshold determination.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical-to-code mapping, the dependence of $P_{	ext{worst } L}$ on $p_{mol}$ for different encodings, and the suppression of logical errors in favored versus disfavored logical sectors as distance increases.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the physical-to-code mapping, then comparing $D=2$ vs. $D=4$ encodings under correlated loss, followed by detailed analysis of how spatial embedding creates directional error asymmetries, and finally comparing different noise models (coherent vs. Pauli twirl) for the exchange interaction.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges the gap between physical hardware realization (molecular arrays) and abstract quantum error correction theory, providing concrete, structure-dependent guidelines for designing fault-tolerant quantum processors.
